The wellness trends shaping marketing in 2026 extend well beyond gyms, spas, and supplements. They are showing up in food, travel, weight management, beauty, mental wellbeing, and the way people evaluate health claims. McKinsey’s 2025 consumer research points to growth in functional nutrition, healthy aging, in-person wellness services, weight management, and mental health, while the Global Wellness Institute estimates the broader wellness economy reached $6.8 trillion in 2024. (McKinsey)

For marketers, the useful question is not whether “wellness” is popular. It is how to make a promise specific enough to be useful and credible. That matters especially in health and wellness marketing, where vague transformation language can quickly outrun the evidence behind a product or service.

At-a-Glance

  • The Global Wellness Institute estimates the wellness economy reached $6.8 trillion in 2024 and projects it could reach about $9.8 trillion by 2029. (Global Wellness Institute)
  • Mental wellness remains a fast-growing part of the broader wellness economy, while younger consumers report high stress and unmet mental-health needs. (McKinsey)
  • Functional nutrition is expanding around benefits such as energy, gut health, immunity, and muscle, bone, and joint support. (McKinsey)
  • GLP-1 use is creating adjacent demand for nutrient-dense foods, digestive support, and muscle-maintenance programs. (McKinsey)
  • In-person wellness services and wellness travel are drawing continued interest, including retreats and boutique fitness. (McKinsey) (Global Wellness Institute)

The Signals Behind 2026 Wellness

  • Consumer demand signals from McKinsey’s 2025 survey of more than 9,000 consumers across China, Germany, the U.K., and the U.S. (McKinsey)
  • Macro context on wellness-economy growth and sector size from the Global Wellness Institute. (Global Wellness Institute)
  • Behavioral shifts marketers can’t ignore: present wellbeing, experience-seeking, and emotional fatigue shaping choices. (Think with Google)

1) The Nervous System Era: Calm becomes the new status signal

“Nervous system care” is useful marketing shorthand for a broader shift toward mindfulness, sleep, stress relief, and immediate wellbeing. In McKinsey’s 2025 U.S. survey, 40% of Gen Z respondents said they felt “almost always stressed,” compared with 23% overall. Google’s 2026 trend forecast separately describes consumers prioritising present wellbeing and more immediate forms of progress. (McKinsey) (Think with Google)

  • Mental wellness is being treated as a daily need state, not a crisis-only category, especially among younger consumers. 
  • Messaging that rewards “small wins” and real-life relief beats transformation language that feels unrealistic right now. (Think with Google)
  • For marketers, calmer creative is most useful when it is paired with a clear benefit rather than generic “wellness” language.

2) Food that does something: Functional nutrition becomes the new default

Functional nutrition is moving closer to everyday food and beverage marketing. McKinsey reports that about half of consumers in the U.S., U.K., and Germany bought functional-nutrition products in the prior year, rising to about two-thirds of Gen Z and millennials. Energy, gut health, immunity, and muscle, bone, and joint support were among the benefits consumers sought. For teams working in food and beverage marketing, that raises the standard for packaging and claims because the product is being asked to communicate a specific function, not just a lifestyle. (McKinsey)

  • Consumers are looking for additive benefits like energy, gut health, and immunity, not just “less bad” versions of old products. 
  • The winners will sit at the intersection of supplements and food, where taste still has to be great. 
  • In wellness trends in marketing, ingredient literacy is becoming a creative advantage, especially for “health traditionalists” who read labels like it’s their job. 

3) The GLP-1 ripple: Weight management becomes an ecosystem

Weight management is also becoming a broader ecosystem. McKinsey points to growing use of prescription weight-loss medications such as GLP-1s and adjacent demand for protein- or nutrient-fortified foods, digestive-support products, and programs focused on maintaining muscle mass. WHO reports that more than one in eight people globally were living with obesity in 2022, which is why marketing in this category needs to avoid reducing a complex health issue to willpower or a before-and-after image. (McKinsey)

WeightWatchers’ 2025 rebrand for the GLP-1 era is one example of how a legacy wellness brand is trying to connect medical, behavioral, community, and digital support under one identity.

  • The GLP-1 era pushes growth in protein and nutrient-fortified foods, gut health support, and muscle maintenance programs. (McKinsey)
  • In McKinsey’s U.S. survey, 44% of Gen Z respondents said staying motivated to exercise was challenging, compared with 37% overall. (McKinsey)
  • The strongest branding services in this category should support clear, evidence-informed language rather than shame-based or overly simplistic messaging. (World Health Organization)

4) Preventive everything: Longevity and beauty merge into healthspan storytelling

Healthy aging and beauty are increasingly overlapping with preventive wellness. McKinsey reports that up to 60% of consumers across surveyed markets consider healthy aging a top or very important priority, and notes that younger consumers are also taking a more proactive approach. The same research points to stronger overlap between beauty, wellness, at-home devices, supplements, and personalized recommendations. (McKinsey)

For marketers, longevity claims still need discipline. A branding agency can help translate a long-term positioning idea into immediate, understandable benefits without implying that branding itself validates a health outcome. Oura’s wellness and health-data positioning shows how design, identity, and measurement can work together while remaining distinct from medical proof.

  • Longevity marketing works better when it leads with immediate benefits like energy and reduced fatigue, not age-based fear. (McKinsey)
  • Beauty-wellness crossover will keep accelerating through partnerships and cross-channel distribution. 
  • McKinsey also identifies gen AI as one opportunity for more personalized beauty and wellness recommendations. (McKinsey)

5) The reset economy goes offline: Experiences, travel, and digital detox

In-person wellness is another important part of the 2026 picture. McKinsey’s 2025 survey found 30% net purchase intent for boutique fitness classes and wellness retreats, while 56% of U.S. in-person service purchasers said they had traveled two or more hours for a wellness retreat. Nearly 60% of consumers who traveled for health and wellness treatments in 2024 said they expected to do so again the following year. The Global Wellness Institute reports wellness-tourism expenditures of $894 billion in 2024. (McKinsey) (Global Wellness Institute)

That creates opportunities in travel and hospitality marketing, but the experience still has to deliver something beyond wellness aesthetics. For brands translating that demand into campaigns, Brand Vision's branding agency can help connect the experience to a clearer promise and customer journey.

  • Experience-led wellness is rising because people want skills and rituals that survive after the trip, not just pretty photos. (McKinsey)
  • Wellness travel is a major spending category, but the definition includes travel associated with maintaining or enhancing personal wellbeing, not only dedicated retreats. (Global Wellness Institute)
  • For organizations adapting these experience ideas locally, a marketing agency in Montreal can help translate the positioning into regional campaigns without assuming the same wellness offer works in every market.

FAQ

What are the top wellness trends of 2026 that matter most for marketing?

The top wellness trends of 2026 that will shape marketing are nervous system care, functional nutrition, the GLP-1 ripple effect in weight management, longevity and preventive aesthetics, and the offline reset economy through experiences and travel. Each one is driven by the same pressure: people want proof and relief, not vague aspiration. 

Why are wellness trends shaping marketing in 2026 so focused on mental wellbeing?

Because younger consumers report high stress and unmet mental-health needs, and many are seeking support through categories that include mindfulness, sleep, fitness, and beauty. McKinsey’s survey found U.S. Gen Z respondents reported “almost always stressed” at a higher rate than the overall sample.

What does functional nutrition mean in 2026?

It means consumers expect food and beverages to deliver specific benefits, like energy, gut support, or immunity, not just calories and taste. McKinsey notes this category is growing and that many consumers, especially Gen Z and millennials, report buying functional nutrition products, with innovation moving toward hybrid products that feel like both food and supplements. 

How is the GLP-1 boom changing wellness trends in marketing?

It’s shifting weight management messaging toward integrated support and practical outcomes, including protein, nutrient fortification, digestive comfort, and muscle maintenance. McKinsey describes a wellness ecosystem forming around GLP-1 users’ needs, which pushes brands to build solutions that feel supportive rather than judgmental. 

Why is wellness travel growing so fast heading into 2026?

McKinsey reports continued interest in retreats and other in-person services, while the Global Wellness Institute estimates wellness-tourism expenditures reached $894 billion in 2024. The category is broad, so marketers should distinguish dedicated wellness retreats from travel that includes wellbeing as one part of the experience.

The New Wellness Contract: What 2026 Marketing Has to Earn

The five trends point in the same direction: people are asking wellness products and experiences to be more specific about what they do, how they fit into daily life, and what evidence supports the promise. Calm, functional benefits, medical-adjacent services, preventive positioning, and offline experiences can all be useful themes, but none replaces clear product value.

Anti-AI marketing moved from a niche stance to a visible creative strategy in 2025. The strongest campaigns did not simply reject technology. They used human authorship, physical experiences, real people, and transparent production choices as signals of trust.

For Brand Vision, these campaigns are most useful as case studies in positioning. They show how brands can respond to AI fatigue without turning the message into fear, and how a clear promise can shape creative direction, channel choices, and customer trust.

At a Glance

  • The anti-AI marketing that worked in 2025 did not argue about tools. It sold a feeling: human presence, imperfection, and real connection.
  • Polaroid turned screen fatigue into a city-wide statement, placing anti-screen and anti-AI messages near tech landmarks and pairing them with phone-free experiences.
  • Aerie made "No AI" a trust promise, extending its long-running no-retouching stance into a clear, modern pledge.
  • Heineken's "real friends" wearable flipped the AI-companionship conversation into an offline invitation, built for culture-speed sharing.
  • The anti-AI slogans that traveled were short and absolute: "Not now, not ever" from DC Comics, "This show was made by humans" from Pluribus, and Heineken's "real friends aren't artificial."
  • The backlash is backed by data: most Americans want clearer AI labeling, and AI-made ads can struggle to stick in memory.

Why people dislike AI in advertising right now

The clearest explanation for why people dislike AI in advertising comes down to trust and perceived authenticity. Many people want more control over how AI appears in daily life and want to know whether content was made by AI or by people. For marketers, that makes transparency part of the message rather than a footnote. Brand research can help identify where AI use affects trust in a specific category instead of assuming every audience responds the same way.

  • Pew Research found that 50% of U.S. adults are more concerned than excited about increased AI use in daily life, and 76% say it is extremely or very important to be able to tell whether pictures, videos, and text were made by AI or by people. (Pew Research Center)
  • NielsenIQ reported that AI-generated ads, even when judged high quality, can show weaker memory activation than traditional ads, which is a technical way of saying they are less likely to stick. (NielsenIQ)
  • CivicScience found that 36% of U.S. adults said they are less likely to buy from a brand that uses AI in its ads, versus 10% who said more likely. (CivicScience)

1) Polaroid: The Camera for an Analog Life

Polaroid did not whisper its point. It put it on walls. The Camera for an Analog Life campaign positioned Polaroid as the antidote to digital overload, pairing real Polaroid photos with copy that calls out screens and AI directly. The placements did the heavy lifting: high-traffic spots near Apple Stores and Google offices, turning the message into a playful confrontation with modern tech habits. Then Polaroid took it past posters with phone-free walking tours, making "log off" something you could actually do, not just a slogan. (Polaroid Newsroom)

  • Positioning: analog life as a response to digital exhaustion and AI noise.
  • The tactic that made it land: high-impact out-of-home placed deliberately near tech landmarks, plus phone-free walking tours.
  • Why it is peak anti-AI marketing: it sells sensory, physical proof an algorithm cannot replicate.

2) Aerie: No retouching. No AI. 100% Aerie Real.

Aerie understood something most brands miss: you can’t “authenticity wash” your way out of an AI backlash; you need a consistent history. Their 2025 message worked because it wasn’t a sudden reinvention; it was a clean extension of a promise they’ve been making since 2014, when they said they stopped retouching bodies. In 2025, they pushed that stance forward with a direct commitment: no AI-generated bodies or people, plus the blunt line that makes it impossible to misread. The response was measurable too, with reporting pointing to major engagement lift and a standout reaction in comments. (Aerie) (Business Insider)

  • The promise in plain language: “no AI-generated bodies or people” tied to the brand’s “Real people only” identity. (Aerie)
  • Reported performance signal: over 40,000 likes on the pledge post and an engagement lift over a two-week window. (Business Insider)
  • Why it’s one of the best anti-AI marketing campaigns: it treats trust like a product feature, not a vibe.

3) Heineken: Real friends aren't artificial

Heineken did not frame the campaign as a ban on AI. Instead, it used the line "real friends aren't artificial" to contrast AI companionship with meeting people in person, supported by a bottle-opener necklace that riffs on wearable-tech culture. The rollout moved through social and high-impact out-of-home in New York. For food and beverage marketing, the useful lesson is how a product can anchor a cultural idea without pretending the technology itself is the enemy. (LBBOnline) (Business Insider)

  • Creative core: a functional bottle-opener necklace presented as a playful social wearable.
  • Message architecture: "real friends" and offline moments, delivered with irony and speed.
  • Why it rode the backlash wave: it piggybacked on public pushback around AI-companionship ads and redirected the conversation into real-world togetherness.

4) Spotify Wrapped 2025: The human comeback, without pretending data isn't the point

Spotify is the clearest example here of a human-centred creative response rather than an anti-AI policy. The 2025 Wrapped campaign described its design as a modern "visual mixtape," mixing analog and digital aesthetics and extending the experience into real-world installations. That makes it relevant to this list because the creative emphasized identity, shared moments, and physical presence while the product itself remained data-driven. (Spotify Newsroom) (MediaPost)

  • Spotify described the 2025 Wrapped design as a visual mixtape, blending analog and digital aesthetics.
  • MediaPost referenced criticism tied to the 2024 Wrapped using generative-AI elements, followed by a bigger, bolder 2025 release.
  • Why it belongs on a list of best anti-AI marketing campaigns: it makes the output feel human even when the engine is still data.

5) DC Comics: The anti-AI pledge as brand protection

This one is not an ad spot, but it is still a public brand promise. DC president and publisher Jim Lee said the company would not support generative AI for storytelling or artwork under current leadership. In entertainment marketing, where authorship and craft are part of the product, that kind of policy can become part of audience trust. (The Verge)

  • The line that spread: "not now, not ever," tied to a commitment to human creativity.
  • Why it plays as anti-AI marketing: it reassures audiences who recoil from creative output that feels fake.
  • What it signals to the market: human authorship is part of the brand's value, not just the production method.

6) Pluribus: "Made by humans" becomes the flex

When a show tucks "This show was made by humans" into its credits, it is doing more than making a statement. It is planting a flag in a cultural argument. In 2025, "made by humans" started behaving like a quality label, the way "handmade" or "small batch" works in other categories. That is why the moment matters to marketers: the phrase is not really about fear of tools, it is reassurance that a real author stands behind what you are watching. It is anti-AI marketing energy, just delivered through entertainment instead of billboards. (Business Insider)

  • The disclaimer: "This show was made by humans," appearing at the end of the credits.
  • Why it resonates inside the backlash: it answers why people dislike AI in advertising and content without a debate, just a signal.
  • The broader takeaway: "human-made" is becoming a story device, not just a production note.

The anti-AI slogans that actually traveled

The strongest anti-AI slogans of 2025 share one trait: they are short, human, and impossible to misread. None of them explains AI. Each one just plants a flag and dares you to check it.

  • "Not now, not ever." DC Comics president Jim Lee, ruling out AI-generated storytelling or artwork.
  • "This show was made by humans." The disclaimer in the credits of Pluribus, now read like a quality label.
  • "Real friends aren't artificial." Heineken, turning AI companionship into an argument for meeting up in person.
  • "No retouching. No AI. 100% Aerie Real." Aerie, treating a no-AI promise as a product feature.
  • "The Camera for an Analog Life." Polaroid, selling presence instead of pixels.

Notice what none of these slogans do. They do not lecture, hedge, or explain the technology. When trust is the product, the slogan is the receipt.

The shared DNA of the best anti-AI marketing campaigns

The strongest examples share a practical pattern: they make the human signal visible. Polaroid used physical photography and offline experiences, Aerie tied the message to real people and its long-running no-retouching stance, and Heineken used a real-world social ritual. (Business Insider) When creators are part of the distribution plan, disciplined influencer marketing planning can help keep that promise consistent across sponsored content instead of turning it into a one-off slogan.

  • Human-made proof beats human-made claims, especially when the audience is already primed by the backlash.
  • Tactile and offline moments act like trust accelerators: out-of-home, physical products, live activations.
  • Clear vows, like "no AI-generated bodies," land harder than vague "we value authenticity" copy.

What business owners can learn from anti-AI marketing in 2026

Anti-AI marketing works best when it is framed as clarity about what customers are buying, not fear of technology. A branding agency can help define which parts of the experience need visible human authorship and which uses of AI should simply be disclosed. FAQ

Is anti-AI marketing actually anti-technology?

Usually no. The strongest anti-AI marketing in 2025 was not saying "never use AI." It was saying "do not replace the human part people came for," especially where authenticity is the whole point. That is why so many campaigns framed the message around connection, real bodies, and real-world experiences rather than technical arguments.

What is the difference between anti-AI marketing and transparency marketing?

Anti-AI marketing uses "human-made" as a positioning advantage. Transparency marketing focuses on disclosure: being clear about what tools were used and where. In practice the line blurs, because a big part of why people dislike AI in advertising is the sense of being tricked, so clear labeling and clear choices do some of the same trust work. The overlap is sharpest in trust-first categories like nonprofit and mission-driven marketing, where audiences expect disclosure by default.

Do people really care if an ad is AI-generated?

A meaningful share does, especially when faces, bodies, or emotional storytelling are involved. Pew's findings show many people want to be able to tell whether something is AI-made or human-made (Pew Research Center), and NielsenIQ's research suggests AI ads can struggle to activate memory the same way (NielsenIQ), which can weaken effectiveness even when the visuals look good.

What makes a good anti-AI slogan?

The anti-AI slogans that worked in 2025 were short, absolute, and free of jargon. Lines like "not now, not ever" and "this show was made by humans" land because they make a promise a person can hold the brand to, not a claim about technology. A good anti-AI slogan names what stays human and dares you to check.

What is the fastest way to apply this without sounding performative?

Start with one verifiable promise you can keep, then show receipts. That might mean a no-AI rule for specific categories like people and bodies, or showing the real creatives and real process behind the work, the way Polaroid and Aerie anchored their campaigns in tangible proof. Make the audience feel the human, not just read about it.

The real win behind the AI backlash

Anti-AI marketing is not winning because people hate technology. It is winning because people hate feeling lonely, manipulated, or bored. The backlash is really a demand for authorship, for proof that someone cared, and for experiences that feel lived-in instead of generated. The best anti-AI marketing campaigns of 2025 did not try to outsmart the algorithm. They reminded people what a human moment feels like, then built the campaign around it.

Human-made is no longer a production note. It is the pitch.

Guerrilla marketing uses an unexpected space, object, or moment to make the placement part of the message. Instead of relying only on a standard media slot, the brand changes how people experience an ordinary environment, whether that is a crosswalk, mall floor, bench, exit sign, sidewalk, or red carpet. The strongest executions are easy to understand in seconds and closely tied to what the brand sells.

These seven best guerrilla marketing examples show different versions of that idea. Some were ambient advertising created by major agencies, while one became a viral sponsorship moment after the cameras started rolling. For startups and small businesses, the lesson is not that every stunt is cheap. Production, permissions, safety, staffing, and measurement still matter. The useful lesson is how creative placement can make a simple idea more memorable.

Mr. Clean Crosswalk

First is the Mr. Clean crosswalk, a widely circulated ambient execution documented in Italy. One stripe of the crosswalk appears dramatically whiter than the others, with the Mr. Clean character attached to the bright stripe. The product benefit is visible before anyone reads a line of copy, turning the street marking into a compact cleaning demonstration.

The strength is the fit between medium and promise. The crosswalk already contains repeated white bars, so changing one bar creates an immediate before-and-after comparison. It is also visually contrasting without needing a long headline. For marketers, the transferable idea is to let graphic design make the product benefit legible at a glance rather than adding decoration after the concept is chosen.

Stepping on Frontline’s Giant Dog

Frontline’s Giant Dog turned mall foot traffic into part of the picture. From above, shoppers walking over a giant dog image looked like fleas. Ads of the World archives the execution as a 2009 ambient campaign by Saatchi & Saatchi Jakarta in Indonesia. The placement mattered as much as the illustration because the idea only fully appeared from the upper levels of the mall.

The campaign is useful because the audience unknowingly completes the visual. It also makes the product problem visible without showing the product itself. Public performance metrics for the original installation are limited, so its value is better understood as a placement and perspective lesson than as an unverified claim about virality. The media choice, viewpoint, and brand problem all work together.

“Irresistible” Axe Body Spray Exit Sign

Sometimes guerrilla marketing focuses on a small intervention rather than a large installation. The Axe Body Spray Exit Man campaign added chasing figures beside a familiar emergency-exit pictogram, turning a standard sign into a joke about attraction. Ads of the World records the execution as a 2007 ambient campaign created by Lowe Belgium. It fit Axe’s longtime brand message: their scents make guys highly appealing to potential love interests.

The execution works because it borrows a visual language people already understand. The added sticker changes the meaning of the sign without requiring a second explanation. It is also a reminder that guerrilla marketing does not have to be physically large. A small intervention can be effective when the brand idea, placement, and audience context are immediately connected.

Orbit Gum Dripping in the Streets

Among the most mouth-watering guerrilla campaigns is Orbit Gum’s “juicy fruit flavor” advertisement. BBDO, the creative agency behind it, decided to make gum so appealing that it would literally appear to spill onto the streets. In certain cities, sidewalk or pavement art showcased bright fruit “juices” seemingly pouring out, as if an enormous piece of gum was melting with fruity goodness. The aim was to convey that Orbit’s gum packs a burst of flavor so intense it’s leaking right out in a fun, eye-catching way.

Ads of the World archives the “Juicy” work as a 2009 ambient campaign by GITAM/BBDO in Israel. Its strength is sensory translation: colour and the illusion of liquid communicate flavour before the audience processes the copy. For food and beverage marketing, that is a useful lesson. The environment can help dramatize taste, texture, or refreshment when the connection is clear and does not depend on an exaggerated product claim.

Kit Kat’s Literal Break

When you think of Kit Kat, you probably recall the slogan “Have a Break, Have a Kit Kat.” Best Ads documents the 2009 ambient execution by JWT London, which turned street benches into objects that resembled giant chocolate bars with segments. The bench already represented a break, while its slatted form could visually echo the product. That gave the campaign a direct connection between object, slogan, and packaging.

The useful principle is message consistency. The product shape, the physical object, and the long-running “break” positioning all reinforce one another. That is stronger than adding a logo to an unrelated installation. It also shows why permissions and execution matter: public furniture, transit areas, and other shared spaces have practical constraints that need to be resolved before the creative idea can work in the real world.

Fiji Girl At The Golden Globes

Guerrilla marketing does not always begin as a street installation. At the 2019 Golden Globes, Fiji Water promotional staff member Kelleth Cuthbert stood on the red carpet with a tray of bottled water, photobombing numerous celebrity pictures. Her repeated appearances in event photography quickly became a meme and turned a normal sponsor presence into a much larger earned-media moment.

The distinction matters because the viral outcome should not be rewritten as a fully planned stunt. The Guardian reported that Cuthbert was part of the brand’s promotional staff and later said she had not deliberately set out to photobomb celebrities. Fiji was able to capitalize on the attention once it happened. For marketers, the lesson is to separate planned placement from earned reaction and evaluate both with appropriate marketing metrics.

Nike’s Bench Advertising

Finally, Nike’s bench execution turned a place associated with rest into a prompt to move. Nike placed or designed a bench in such a way that the seat portion was removed, leaving the back structure with the Swoosh and “RUN.” The One Club credits the 2012 “Special Bench” work to F/Nazca Saatchi & Saatchi in São Paulo.

The bench works because it reverses the expected function of the object while staying consistent with Nike’s movement-oriented brand strategy. The viewer understands the joke before needing an explanation. It is also a useful reminder that a strong ambient idea is not just “unexpected.” The surprise has to point back to a recognizable brand promise.

What Makes Guerrilla Marketing So Effective

Across these examples, the common principle is contextual fit. Mr. Clean uses a white stripe, Frontline uses people as “fleas,” Kit Kat uses the idea of a break, and Nike turns rest into movement. Surprise earns the first look, but the connection to the brand is what gives the execution meaning. Brand Vision’s guide to guerrilla marketing tactics for local businesses applies the same principle to smaller, more practical activations.

For a real campaign, creative concepting is only one part of the work. Teams also need permission to use the space, safe production, a plan for documentation, and a way to measure what happened after launch. Local context matters too. A street activation in Miami, for example, has to fit the property, weather, pedestrian flow, tourism patterns, and neighborhood rather than borrowing a stunt from another city unchanged. A Miami marketing team can help adapt an idea to that market, while a broader marketing agency can connect the activation to the rest of the campaign.

Content marketing is one of the best ways to promote your business. Without it, you cannot expect to make many sales. But the challenge lies in picking your tactics and formulating a marketing strategy. For the finest outcomes, you have to take the right approach when it comes to marketing your product. 

Unfortunately, there's no one-size-fits-all solution for increasing brand awareness. In this article, we will examine some methods to get acquainted with your audience and effectively engage them.

‍

Get to Know Your Buyer

Performing marketing research is essential. Learn who your potential customers are, what problem they need to solve and what it is that makes them click that 'buy now' button.

Just as professional essay writers for hire can write your essay for money, you can hire a marketing professional to do that research for you. But, obviously, all the expenses can add up to a pretty lump sum. At first, many businesses cannot afford to spend any extra money, even on essentials like market research. Opting to do it on your own is a viable option, too.

Identify Your Customer

Determine who your product is for and why they need to buy from you. Create a buyer persona, a generalized idea of your perfect customer. It can be a Gen-Z woman who is looking for an eco-conscious makeup brand or an elderly man who needs a universal pair of glasses.

Engage People Into Research

Use your personas as a guide and look for those people in real life. Approach your past customers or potential ones. You can find them among your competitors' social media following. For maximum depth of your market research, aim for people of different ages, income levels, genders and family statuses. This will give you the most diverse group, hence more data to work with. In exchange for their time, offer them a reward. It can be money or your products.

Prepare a Questionnaire

Thoroughly preparing the questions is half the success. You need to ask your participants open-ended questions that will allow for the most independent and unbiased answers. The tentative line of questioning should be as follows: 

  • How and when did you realize you had a problem that needed to be solved?
  • How did you research potential solutions?
  • What influenced your decision to buy or leave the site/store?

Expand these to be more specific and relevant to your niche or brand. Once the questionnaire is finished, ensure that you thank your participants.

Research Your Competitors

Check your competitors' social media, website, and general online presence. Take note of whether they operate offline or not, i.e., if they have a physical store or an office. This will show you the full picture of what your potential customers expect.

Look at their following-to-engagement ratio. Do they have many followers and few likes, or the opposite? Do they follow trends and post viral content? How can you make your content viral as well?

Notice if they post more videos or more photos on their pages. Does that ratio change depending on the platform? How much product photography do they post, and does it get the same engagement?

Answering all these questions will help you build your own social media tactics. A content marketing agency can assist in analyzing competitor strategies and crafting a unique content approach tailored to your audience. By understanding what works in your industry, you can refine your marketing strategy and drive more engagement

Brand Awareness

The initial stage of improving your brand awareness is developing a style. The style of your social media depends on your buyer persona.

For the sake of this blog post, we will assume that your customer is a Gen-Z woman. She's a student, works a part-time job and gets occasional support from her parents. She's conscious of ecology and interested in politics. She thrifts most of her clothes or buys from small brands. She likes things that are made to last but does occasionally buy fast fashion due to convenience. 

You can't resell AliExpress accessories and expect her to become your loyal customer. For her to become a repeat customer, she needs to see the manufacturing process and be sure you're not just another reseller.

‍

How to Develop a Style?

The key to being easily recognized by your followers is sticking to a creative copywriting strategy, aesthetic or vision. If you're posting product photography, make sure that it's identifiable by more than a label. Take pictures in nature on diverse models or put certain filters on all the images.

The viewer has to see your post and recognize your style before they see who posted it. This is what brand awareness is. 

Research keywords relevant to your brand on Pinterest to see what your audience wants to see. For our Gen-Z customer, you could try'slow fashion,' 'upcycling,' 'natural fabrics,' etc. Use your findings as references when developing your branding strategy.

Transparency is Key

Progress videos get lots of hits across most social media platforms. Artisans who make accessories, clothes or food from scratch get millions of followers. If you need Gen Z to interact with your content, you should show how your product is made.

If the product is mass-produced, it's important to have a transparent and clean sourcing process. Saying that you get your materials from a sustainable source but not having any proof of that just won't cut it anymore. Most people, and especially Gen Z, who have lots of buying power, care deeply about where their stuff comes from. This is why they are canceling brands for greenwashing and lack of transparency. Sure, they might indulge occasionally, like they do with Shein, but they are not loyal customers.

To foster loyalty, you have to build a personal rapport with your followers. Don't treat them as potential customers. Instead, try to have a relatable image. Show your everyday work processes and struggles, and talk about challenges openly. 

Put a Face Behind the Brand

One of the reasons why Rihanna's Fenty Beauty is so popular is obviously because she is Rihana. But another reason is that she appears in the brand's content regularly. She uses the products she advertises, which builds customer trust and loyalty. 

Most recent influencer scandals involve influencers not using advertised products. Followers perceive this behavior as a blatant lie and are less willing to trust that influencer in the future. This is why micro-influencers have such a wide reach these days. 

People with 10,000 followers or less are considered micro-influencers. Unlike those with a million followers or more, these micro-influencers have a tighter community of followers. The followers are usually more engaged and trust the creator more. They feel like a part of their lives since the creator interacts with the followers' comments. This builds trust between the creator and their community, and for advertisers, this is a goldmine. 

Offering your product, a discount code or an exclusive offer to a creator with a smaller audience can yield better results for a smaller price. Besides, influencers with a smaller following are usually more responsive, sometimes even more reliable and are easier to work with.

Use User-Generated Content

Motivate buyers to post content with your products. They can share a review or a video of them using your product or service. In return, you give them a discount for the next purchase. Having pinned stories with customer reviews on your Instagram also improves the trustworthiness of your brand. While browsing or researching to buy, someone will see how many customers have bought from you and trust you more. 

Reposting those reviews may also convince those people who follow you but are still on the fence about making a purchase. 

However, make sure to post user-generated content in moderation. Some people may follow you for the aesthetic value and will unfollow you if you post random people's selfies all the time.

‍

Engage With Your Followers

Interacting with your followers is paramount to building trust and a sense of community around your brand. Write questions in your posts to prompt people to comment. Reply to those comments and like them to make people feel seen.

If they criticize the branding, product quality or any other aspect, take it into consideration. They might have a point. And if you edit your product with people's comments in mind, they will be more inclined to buy from you.

On Instagram, you can post questions and polls or answer people's DMs publicly. This will paint a more reliable image of your brand. On TikTok, you can reply to comments with videos, which is also a very effective branding tool. 

Wrapping up

Developing proper branding is paramount in the current business environment. Without it, you will be just another brand that nobody cares about. But you must put your work into it to make the branding efficient. 

For that, perform thorough market research. Develop your buyer persona, conduct interviews with potential customers and analyze the results. Perform competitor research. See what they are doing well and what missteps you can avoid. Interact with your audience by posting user-generated content and replying to comments. Take feedback into account and use it for growth and development.

As visual marketing takes the global digital economies by storm, user-generated content has seen to become a must have in every marketing team's arsenal. Did you know? Leveraging real-time customer voices through user-generated content is seen to not only build trust and authenticity, but additionally boost interactions and engagements significantly.

The most common question that comes to mind when getting started with user-generated content is, to what extent does UGC marketing prove effective? Join us as this article explores the extent to which artificial intelligence can potentially enhance your organization's marketing efforts and take engagements and conversions to new heights.

Understanding User-Generated Content

Put in simple terms, user-generated content is any type of content that is inclusive of not only text and images but also videos and product reviews that are created of the people, by the people for the people, rather than the brands themselves.

Seen to be one of the most authentic forms of content marketing, UGC utilises videos that showcase real users sharing their reviews and experiences with your products or services. This proves to be beneficial as organizations and brands can create more content that is not only engaging but resonates with the dynamic demands of your targeted audiences. More relatable content is additionally seen to spread rapidly through word of mouth and peer recommendations.

The role of AI in ugc marketing

Now that User-generated content is understood, let's explore the role of AI in this field of marketing. AI is seen to offer brands and organizations with the ability to not only create content, but also analyze data to provide personalized experiences to audiences. Let's explore how AI can transform your UGC marketing strategy.

Content discovery and curation

One of the key difficulties when it comes to acquiring UGC is finding relevant content that aligns with your brands values and customers needs. With the help of AI algorithms, your organization has the ability to effortlessly scan and analyze a vast number of data points across social media channels while reviewing different sites in order to identify those high quality UGC videos that are aligned with your brands messages. Taking advantage of tools that feature image recognition alongside natural language processing (NLP) can benefit your organization when it comes to being able to curate and showcase impactful UGC.

Enhancing quality of content

These AI tools also have the ability to provide improvements in UGC, removing filler words and segments to provide clarity and state of flow while maintaining the authentic nature of the creator's tone. Personalizing customer experiences

When it comes to the dynamic needs of customers, personalization is seen to be pivotal when it comes to a winning marketing strategy. Keeping this in mind, AI has the power to not only analyze the behavior and preferences of users but also, personalize UGC content to make it relevant to diverse audience segments. By identifying the type of content that resonates with audience segments, AI can be leveraged to fine tune marketing campaigns to meet individual interests and boost conversion rates.

Predictive analytics

Predictive analytics is another distinguishable feature of AI based UGC marketing. Powered by AI, predictive analytics involves forecasting both trends as well as consumers behavior in order to anticipate future trends. This creates room for organizations to be proactive when it comes to creating campaigns around emerging trends.

Automating campaign management

Emily in Paris Season 5 collaborations show how entertainment can turn attention into a consumer journey, from on-screen product placement to pop-ups and limited drops. The strongest examples connect a recognizable story moment to a clear product, event, or next step.

For marketers, the lesson is not limited to fashion or consumer products. The pattern can apply wherever a brand has a narrative, a community, and an offer that can be tied naturally to a cultural moment. Season 5 makes those mechanics visible across product placement, retail activations, limited releases, and the digital experiences that connect them.

This review focuses on the Emily in Paris brand partnerships that were publicly tied to the Season 5 release window and supported with activation. It is designed to be used as a practical reference, not a recap.

At a Glance: The Confirmed Season 5 Brand Collaborations

Below are the Season 5 brand collaborations most clearly positioned as consumer-facing partnerships around the Season 5 launch.

  • Fendi: A plot-led integration paired with a capsule-style product release. (Fendi and Emily in Paris)
  • Intimissimi: A storyline-forward feature designed to feel natural on screen while remaining easy to merchandise off screen. (Intimissimi Brings Italian Elegance to Emily in Paris Season 5)
  • Boursin: A real-world pop-up experience in Toronto that turns a streaming moment into an in-person event. (Boursin Bistro pop-up experience)
  • Planet Oat: A limited-edition creamer tied to premiere timing, retail distribution, and a pop-up moment. (Planet Oat x Emily in Paris creamer)
  • Baked by Melissa: A limited-time drop that is easy to explain, easy to gift, and easy to share. Baked by Melissa x Emily in Paris Season 5

These Emily in Paris Season 5 collaborations work because they keep the consumer decision simple. Each partnership gives fans a clear next action that is not vague brand affinity. It is a product, an event, or both.

Fendi: Plot-Led Product Placement and a Capsule Collection

What Happened

Fendi is the clearest example of a collaboration built into narrative structure. Season 5 does not simply feature a product. The brand is used as a plot device, which changes how viewers process the placement.

At the same time, Fendi supported the on-screen integration with a consumer-facing selection tied to the show. The brand presented the products as part of the same story world, not as separate merchandising. (Fendi and Emily in Paris)

Relevant source coverage also points to a release timed to the Season 5 premiere window and supported through press appearances and product storytelling. (Vogue)

Why It Works

Fendi works as an integration because the placement has a narrative role rather than functioning as background signage. That makes the product part of the scene’s logic and gives the audience a clearer reason to remember it.

From a marketing lens, this is a strong example of Season 5 brand collaborations following three principles:

  • Context first: The product belongs in the scene.
  • One hero object: The audience can name what they saw.
  • A direct path to purchase: Fans can find the product without effort.

This is also a clean example of Emily in Paris brand partnerships aligning the show’s visual language with the brand’s retail language. It keeps continuity across screen, social, and storefront.

What Brands Can Borrow

Most brands will not have a Fendi-level storyline. The transferable part is the structure.

Use this checklist when planning an entertainment collaboration:

  • Define a single hero product or offer that can be understood in one sentence.
  • Ensure the product can be discovered in under 30 seconds from any social post.
  • Align creative assets across show moment, brand channels, and product page photography.

If the campaign requires a new product page or a temporary microsite, treat it as a real conversion surface. Work with a web design agency early, not after creative is locked. The campaign will be judged on speed, clarity, and checkout integrity as much as it is judged on aesthetics.

Fendi shows how product placement can connect storytelling to a purchase path when the consumer journey is designed end to end.

Intimissimi: Storyline Integration That Feels Shoppable

What Happened

Intimissimi’s approach is direct: feature the brand prominently in a way that matches setting and character behavior. The integration is positioned as part of the season’s Italian setting and style cues, and it is presented as a meaningful on-screen moment rather than a casual background detail. (Intimissimi Brings Italian Elegance to Emily in Paris Season 5)

This is a different category of Season 5 brand collaborations than a retail pop-up. It is closer to a shoppable wardrobe moment, where brand recognition and fit are the primary levers.

Why It Works

Intimissimi benefits from three conditions that make Emily in Paris brand partnerships perform:

  • High visual clarity: The product category reads immediately on screen.
  • Low explanation burden: The audience does not need instruction to understand what it is.
  • Private utility: Consumers can buy the item without signaling fandom publicly.

That last point matters. Many entertainment tie-ins rely on obvious branding. Intimissimi’s category allows a quieter purchase motive. The product can be bought for personal reasons and still be linked to the show’s aesthetic.

What Brands Can Borrow

If your product can plausibly be part of daily life, you can replicate this model without forcing a branded punchline.

Execution guidance:

  • Design product pages around materials, fit, and use, not around references to the show.
  • Create a curated collection page with tight merchandising. Ten products are often enough.
  • Build an editorial layer that explains “where and why” without spoilers.

This is where UI UX design agency work becomes practical. The path to purchase should be predictable, with strong imagery and clear sizing and return information. Those fundamentals make the collaboration easier to shop without turning the product page into campaign clutter.

Intimissimi is one of the Emily in Paris Season 5 collaborations that highlights a core truth: the easiest collaborations to scale are the ones that do not require the customer to perform fandom in public.

Boursin: A Pop-Up Experience Built for Social Sharing

What Happened

Boursin created a physical activation tied to the Season 5 moment: the Boursin Bistro pop-up at Café Renée in Toronto. The event was framed as an Emily in Paris inspired experience, designed for a one-night window and built around reservable attendance. (Boursin Bistro pop-up experience)

This is a strong example of Emily in Paris brand partnerships using scarcity and place. It converts a streaming premiere into a reason to go out, take photos, and share.

Why It Works

Boursin’s activation is effective because it does not ask the audience to buy an abstract feeling. It offers an experience with clear constraints:

  • Date and time are fixed.
  • Entry is gated by reservations.
  • The product is the center of the menu, not a background sponsor.

For marketers, the transferable lesson is that an event can function as a distribution channel. It can create content and community proof, while a defined measurement plan can connect the activation to outcomes such as reservations, trial, sign-ups, or retail demand. For food and beverage marketing, that link between experience and the next purchase is especially important.

What Brands Can Borrow

If you are planning a pop-up tied to entertainment, treat it like a product launch, not a party.

A practical operational checklist:

  1. Build a single landing page that answers logistics in one screen.
  2. Create a photo plan. Decide what guests will photograph and where.
  3. Ensure the brand moment is in the path, not only on signage.
  4. Capture emails or opt-ins ethically and clearly.
  5. Define post-event conversion. Is it retail purchase, subscriptions, or trial?

Boursin’s program also shows why local execution matters. If the activation is city-based, the creative and logistics should match local expectations and venue realities. Teams coordinating national and regional rollouts may need both consistent branding and Canadian branding support so the core idea stays recognizable without ignoring local context.

Boursin demonstrates a simple idea: experiential work is strongest when the audience experience and the measurement plan are designed together.

Planet Oat: A Retail Product Drop Timed to the Premiere

What Happened

Planet Oat launched a limited-edition creamer tied directly to the season’s premiere timing. The partnership included retail distribution and a pop-up experience aligned to the premiere date, plus talent support through Ashley Park. (Planet Oat x Emily in Paris creamer)

This is a classic “watch moment” product strategy. It turns a household ritual into a purchase that feels relevant for the week the show drops.

Why It Works

Planet Oat’s collaboration works because it fits the natural rhythm of audience behavior:

  • People host watch nights.
  • People shop for groceries weekly.
  • People look for small add-ons that make the moment feel planned.

Among Emily in Paris Season 5 collaborations, this is one of the cleanest examples of meeting fans where they already are. It also shows the value of pairing retail availability with a narrative wrapper.

What Brands Can Borrow

If your product has household frequency, you can use a similar model even without mass retail.

Key execution moves:

  • Use campaign packaging design and naming that read instantly in a store aisle.
  • Build a “where to buy” module that is accurate and mobile-first.
  • Plan for customer support volume during the first seven days.
  • Prepare a short content kit for retailers, not only for your own channels.

This is also where search demand matters. Limited products tied to a cultural moment can create short windows of high-intent branded search. A strong SEO agency partner can help the landing experience capture that demand with clear structure and internal pathways, without turning the page into a cluttered ad.

Planet Oat shows how a modest product drop can still create a clear campaign moment when timing and distribution match an existing consumer routine.

Baked by Melissa: A Limited-Time Drop With Clear Creative Constraints

What Happened

Baked by Melissa released a limited-time Season 5 collection built around a small set of Paris-inspired cupcake flavors. It was positioned as a shareable purchase tied to the season’s release. (Baked by Melissa Season 5 collection)

This is an e-commerce friendly version of a partnership. It does not require retail negotiations or venue production. It requires product storytelling, checkout clarity, and fulfillment readiness.

Why It Works

Baked by Melissa benefits from constraints that make Season 5 brand collaborations easier to execute:

  • The offer is limited and easy to summarize.
  • The product is designed for sharing.
  • The visual language is built into the product itself.

It also fits how audiences behave during releases. They buy small items that signal participation, often for gatherings.

What Brands Can Borrow

The Baked by Melissa model can be adapted by many categories because it is simple.

A useful blueprint:

  • Keep the assortment tight. Too many options dilute the connection.
  • Use photography that looks like editorial, not like a coupon page.
  • Add a “shipping cutoff” module and inventory transparency.
  • Make gifting frictionless, including a clear note field and delivery expectations.

If your current e-commerce experience struggles under traffic spikes, do not wait for the next collaboration to test performance. For teams coordinating identity and conversion at the same time, a branding agency can help keep the campaign promise consistent across creative and the purchase journey. A marketing consultation and audit can also surface conversion and operational issues before launch.

Baked by Melissa is one of the Emily in Paris Season 5 collaborations that shows how a limited drop can succeed when it is operationally calm and visually coherent.

Other Notable Season 5 Brand Integrations Worth Studying

Some Season 5 brand collaborations show up as on-screen integrations that may not have the same consumer product layer as the examples above. They still matter, because they reveal how the show builds a branded world.

The examples below were cited as Season 5 placements in coverage of the season’s marketing and episodes. (Vogue)

Dolce and Gabbana

The brand appears as part of the character world and retail environment. The key lesson is simple: retail locations and shopping scenes are high-leverage moments for lifestyle alignment.

For marketers, the takeaway is not about copying a designer label. It is about using the right “place” as the message. The store becomes the proof point.

Rimowa suitcases were referenced as being present across episodes. Luggage is a functional product with high visual recognition, which makes it a natural fit for travel-driven storytelling.

This is a useful reminder that functional categories can win in entertainment when the object is distinctive and easy to recognize at a glance.

For brands in this category, the core question is whether the product belongs in the moment as a natural choice. If the answer is unclear, the integration usually reads as paid placement.

These integrations are not the same as the headline Emily in Paris Season 5 collaborations listed earlier. They are still relevant for planning, because they show how narrative context shapes audience tolerance for brand presence.

They also reinforce a consistent point about Emily in Paris brand partnerships: context matters. Brand presence is easier to understand when it fits the character, setting, and action already taking place.

The Marketing Tactic Behind Emily in Paris Season 5 Collaborations

The common tactic across the strongest Emily in Paris Season 5 collaborations is not product placement alone. It is a story-to-shelf system with a short, timed conversion window. That same logic is useful in entertainment marketing, where the campaign idea, audience moment, and destination need to reinforce one another.

Season 5 brand collaborations succeed when they connect three layers:

  • A narrative moment that earns attention.
  • A consumer artifact that is easy to buy, book, or share.
  • A distribution plan that meets audiences across platforms.

This is what gives these partnerships an advantage over a disconnected placement: the cultural moment and the next action are designed as one experience.

The Collaboration Stack

Use this stack to plan Season 5 brand collaborations in your own category:

  1. On-screen or cultural trigger
    A scene, a premiere week, a cast appearance, or a storyline moment.
  2. Consumer offer
    Product drop, curated collection, pop-up, bundle, or limited packaging.
  3. Commerce surface
    Landing page, PDP template, store locator, reservation flow, or retailer page.
  4. Distribution layer
    Owned email and social, creator content, retail channels, PR, and partners.
  5. Retention layer
    Capture data where appropriate, then follow up with value, not noise.

Brands that treat this as one system avoid a common failure mode: strong awareness with a weak next step. For a different entertainment mechanic, Netflix’s interactive slate campaign used guided discovery to turn a release announcement into an experience.

If you want examples outside this show, Brand Vision has covered the mechanics of entertainment-led campaigns across categories, including how partnerships go viral and what makes them repeatable.  (2025 in Review: Top 10 Collaborations That Went Viral)

The Measurement Plan

Season 5 brand collaborations are often judged with vague language. That is risky. Entertainment partnerships can deliver real performance, but only if measurement is specified upfront.

A practical measurement plan should include:

  • Branded search lift during premiere week
  • Landing page conversion rate and bounce rate
  • Retail velocity where applicable
  • Earned media volume and quality
  • Incremental email or SMS opt-ins
  • Post-campaign repurchase rate for new customers

For broader context on how Netflix builds global attention and how brands can learn from that distribution discipline, see this breakdown from Brand Vision. (Netflix Marketing Strategy 2025)

A final note on measurement: fans notice when placements feel like ads. Vogue’s coverage of Season 5 highlighted both the commercial upside and the audience sensitivity to overt marketing. That tension is part of the job now. (Vogue)

Collaboration UX: Landing Pages, Checkout, and Accessibility

Season 5 brand collaborations create short spikes of intense intent. That is a website stress test.

If your collaboration landing page loads slowly, hides key details, or breaks on mobile, you will pay for awareness you cannot convert. This is where execution discipline matters more than clever taglines.

For deeper context on how product placement and brand integration work as marketing systems, see: Iconic Brands in Movies: The Art of Product Placement

Make the Drop Page Fast

A collaboration page should behave like a performance page, not like a campaign poster.

Minimum requirements:

  • Load fast on cellular data
  • Clear CTA above the fold
  • Delivery and returns visible without scrolling through long copy
  • Inventory transparency when stock is limited
  • A single primary action per screen

This is also why teams involve a web design agency early. The job is not only layout. It is performance engineering, content structure, and release governance.

Reduce Friction at Checkout

A good collaboration is often a first purchase. That means low trust and high questions.

Reduce friction by standardizing:

  • Guest checkout
  • Express pay options
  • Clear shipping timelines
  • Minimal form fields
  • Mobile-first error handling

If the experience includes reservations or ticketing, apply the same principle. Every unnecessary step is an exit.

Design for Accessibility and Governance

Season 5 brand collaborations attract a broad audience. Accessibility is not optional, and neither is governance.

Practical standards:

  • High contrast text on imagery
  • Keyboard navigability
  • Alt text for key images
  • Clear error messages
  • Version control for landing pages and disclaimers

A UI UX design agency should also be thinking about maintainability. If you run multiple collaborations per year, you need templates, not one-off builds. Templates reduce risk and lower time to market.

The best Emily in Paris brand partnerships look effortless. Behind the scenes, they are operationally strict.

Risks and Guardrails: When Entertainment Partnerships Backfire

Season 5 brand collaborations also show what can go wrong.

Common risks include:

  • Narrative mismatch: Viewers sense a placement that does not belong.
  • Overexposure: Too many branded moments can make a show feel transactional.
  • Inventory gaps: A drop goes viral, then stock disappears with no backorder plan.
  • Unclear rights: Talent, likeness, and title usage can create legal exposure.
  • Tracking blind spots: A campaign succeeds in awareness but cannot be attributed.

Guardrails that protect both brand and partner:

  1. Define the partnership positioning: what must be true for the collaboration to feel credible.
  2. Limit the number of hero messages. One is usually enough.
  3. Align legal, product, and site operations before creative goes live.
  4. Build a post-launch response plan for customer support and community.

If your collaboration is intended to support search growth, not only social reach, coordinate SEO and editorial early. The goal is to capture demand while it is highest, then retain it with evergreen content and internal pathways. A capable SEO agency can help structure that system without compromising brand clarity.

Emily in Paris Season 5 collaborations are effective because they are integrated. They fail when marketing, operations, and digital experience are treated as separate workstreams.

Key Takeaways for Brands Planning 2026 Collaborations

Emily in Paris Season 5 collaborations offer a useful model for modern partnership marketing. The strongest examples are structured around a clear role for the brand, a simple next action, and a customer journey that supports the campaign idea.

The practical lessons are:

  • Season 5 brand collaborations work when there is a single hero offer and a short path to action.
  • Emily in Paris brand partnerships succeed when the product belongs in the story world and the buying experience is predictable.
  • Physical activations are strongest when they create content and conversion, not only ambiance.
  • Limited drops win when fulfillment and customer support are treated as part of the campaign.
  • The website is not a brochure during launch week. It is the campaign.

If you are planning entertainment-led partnerships in 2026, start with fundamentals. Validate your offer, your conversion path, and your operational readiness before you spend on awareness.

Selena Gomez launched Rare Beauty in 2020 around a simple idea: makeup should help people feel like themselves rather than push one narrow standard of perfection. The brand quickly became a major consumer beauty brand, combining prestige retail distribution, direct ecommerce, founder-led storytelling and a mental-health mission. This analysis looks at the Rare Beauty marketing strategy, its business model and the financial evidence that can actually be supported.

Rare Beauty Business Model and Positioning

Rare Beauty built its business through a mix of direct-to-consumer sales and large beauty retail partners, with Sephora playing a central role in its early global distribution. That model gives the company both retail discovery and its own digital customer relationship. For beauty brands, the same mix raises practical UI/UX design questions around shade discovery, product education and conversion, while strong cosmetic branding keeps the product system recognizable across shelves, social content and ecommerce.

The product position sits between mass-market cosmetics and luxury beauty. The company emphasizes easy application, inclusive shade options and a recognizable visual system rather than prestige through scarcity. Rare Beauty’s Liquid Touch foundation and concealer each launched in 48 shades, while the broader Rare Beauty products range has expanded well beyond complexion.

  • Direct ecommerce and retail distribution reduce dependence on a single shopping path.
  • The brand message centers on self acceptance, connecting product positioning with the founder’s public narrative.
  • Its clean typography, soft color system and distinctive packaging make visual identity part of product recognition.

Financial Performance and Valuation Context

The strongest public evidence does not support describing Rare Beauty as a verified $2.7 billion company in 2025. The Business of Fashion reported that Rare Beauty crossed $400 million in net sales in the 12 months ending in February 2024. TIME later reported roughly $400 million in annual sales and a widely cited $2 billion valuation estimate in 2024.

That valuation needs a date attached. Axios reported in September 2024 that a sale process had been paused and cautioned that the company had not established a $2 billion transaction value. Earlier reporting also showed that Rare Beauty had explored strategic options, so the old claim that Gomez simply declined outside investment was too categorical.

  • Rare Beauty had crossed about $400 million in annual or trailing-12-month sales by 2024, depending on the reporting period.
  • TIME described the Soft Pinch Liquid Blush as a major revenue driver, but the original article’s undated three-million-unit claim has been removed.
  • Private-company valuation estimates should be treated as historical reporting, not a current audited value.

Marketing Strategy and Community Building

Rare Beauty’s social presence is closely tied to founder visibility, creator demonstrations and everyday product use. Rather than relying only on polished campaign films, the brand frequently uses tutorials, short-form video and community-led content. That approach fits a broader marketing strategy in which social proof and product education reinforce one another.

Selena Gomez’s role matters, but the brand also has to work when she is not in the frame. Creator content across different skin tones and use cases helps demonstrate the product, while mental-health messaging gives the brand a subject beyond makeup. For teams evaluating whether that positioning is genuinely resonating, structured brand research can separate audience evidence from social-media anecdotes.

  • Founder tutorials make the celebrity connection feel closer to product use than a conventional endorsement.
  • Creator demonstrations give shoppers practical information about shade, texture and application.
